extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of natural philosophy, social theory, and comparative sociology
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition arguing that evolution is an increase of complexity that ends in equilibration, and that dissolution (decay/disintegration) follows from external inputs of motion; includes applications to societies, organisms, inorganic aggregates, and cosmic bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibration as endpoint of evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The establishment of this equilibrium, is the arrival at a state of human nature and social organization, such that the individual has no desires but those which may be satisfied without exceeding his proper sphere of action; while society maintains no restraints but those which the individual voluntarily respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress toward this state is effected by the progressive extension of citizens' liberty and the reciprocal removal of political restrictions; ultimate abolition of all limits to individual freedom (save those imposed by the like freedom of all) results from complete equilibration between desires and surrounding conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase of heterogeneity until equilibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Each new function (internal action) established in evolution implies an increase of heterogeneity; increase of heterogeneity must go on while there remain any outer relations affecting the organism which are unbalanced by inner relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evolution consists in adding internal actions/structures answering previously unknown external relations; the process continues until internal and external relations are balanced—so a satisfactory theory must link new functions/structures to external relations and show how heterogeneity ceases as equilibrium is approached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of force entails motion under resistance and eventual quiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: From the persistence of force follows that attractive and repulsive forces are co-existent and that all motion is motion under resistance; therefore motions are continually dissipated and equilibration must eventually be reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument rests on the necessity of equal and opposite correlatives to any force-experience and on the fact that motion communicated to a resisting medium deducts from the moving body's motion. A correct account should deduce equilibration from the persistence of force and the universal presence of resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability and re-establishment of moving equilibria
rubrics_metrics.description: When a moving equilibrium is disturbed by new motion, either (a) the new motion is of such kind and amount that it cannot be dissipated before the pre-existing motions (bringing the equilibrium to an end), or (b) it can be dissipated before the pre-existing motions (in which case the moving equilibrium is re-established).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields a tendency to conservation of moving equilibria; explanations should compare magnitudes of motions and resistances to predict whether equilibrium will persist or be destroyed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolution defined as disintegration caused by external addition of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissolution is a disintegration of matter, caused by the reception of additional motion from without.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account of dissolution must identify external sources of motion (e.g., aggression, shocks, heat, mechanical action) and show how receipt of such motion converts integrated motions of wholes into motions of parts, producing disintegration across social, organic, inorganic, and cosmic aggregates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social dissolution: decrease of integrated movements, increase of disintegrated movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Social dissolution is, materially considered, a disintegration, and, dynamically considered, a decrease in the movements of wholes and an increase in the movements of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include conquest, plague, revolution; good social-theoretical accounts should trace how external shocks break coordination (political, industrial, commercial) and lead to more local/uncombined transactions and individual movements (emigration, decline in multiplication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of external influences in social change (oscillation and moderation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts between Conservatism (restraints of society over the individual) and Reform (liberty of the individual against society) fall within slowly approximating limits so that temporary predominance of either produces less marked deviation from the medium state; oscillations become more moderate as equilibration progresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social theory should account for oscillatory dynamics and a long-term attenuation of extremes, explaining mechanisms by which opposing forces temper each other and approach a stable balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic dissolution depends on absorption of molecular motion; temperature controls rate
rubrics_metrics.description: In organic dissolution, decomposition (disintegration into gases, increased insensible movements) requires molecular motion supplied from the environment; low temperatures (below freezing) prevent decomposition, while higher temperatures accelerate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evidence: frozen carcasses preserved for millennia; decomposition faster in tropics; cooking causes rapid decomposition and charring. Explanations of decay should emphasize molecular-motion transfer, temperature dependence, and conversion of integrated molecular rhythms into diffused gaseous motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inorganic dissolution via absorption of motion and mechanical action
rubrics_metrics.description: Many inorganic dissolutions (evaporation, volatilization, solution, erosion) involve absorption of motion from the environment; soluble substances dissolve more rapidly in hotter water, and solution is often accompanied by a fall of temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: evaporation of water, wasting of volatile solids (carbonate of ammonia), dissolution of salts (endothermic solution observed as temperature fall), mechanical attrition of strata by waves/glaciers. A correct account should link type of dissolution to source and mode of motion absorption (molecular vs. mechanical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cosmic (universal) dissolution by progressive energy dissipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Over immense times, aggregates like the Earth will be exposed to contingencies that communicate sufficient motion to cause their complete disintegration (e.g., orbital retardation by ethereal resistance leading to fusion/vaporization when falling into the Sun).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses Helmholtz-type calculations and the idea of progressive integration of the Solar System; theories of universal fate must consider energy transformations (molar to molecular motion), resistance of the medium, and cumulative effects that eventually radiate excess motion into space.
